newsitem.title: GERMANY: CYCLING-GERMANS ACCLAIM TOUR KING ULLRICH.
newsitem.headline: CYCLING-GERMANS ACCLAIM TOUR KING ULLRICH.

text.p: Thousands of jubilant, flag-waving Germans packed Bonn's main square on Monday to acclaim Tour de France king Jan Ullrich.
The first German ever to win the world's greatest cycle race seemed taken by surprise at the hero's welcome he received a day after his triumph on the Champs-Elysees.
"I didn't expect there would be so many people," said Ullrich. "It's very touching."
An estimated 10,000-strong crowd had waited for him on a sunny morning on Bonn's Marktplatz, overlooked by the city's monumental town hall.
They burst into applause, waving pink flags and caps handed out by Ullrich's team sponsor Deutsche Telekom, when he climbed the building's stairs and stood on the balcony.
He and his team mates had earlier attended a crowded reception in Telekom's Bonn headquarters.
Ullrich burst into the limelight with perfect timing, providing a new face for the sports media just as some of the stalwarts of the past decade are winding down.
Boris Becker is close to the end of his tennis career while Steffi Graf is struggling with injury in hers.
Ullrich has attracted new superlatives almost every day over the past few weeks, from giant to "Tourminator."
On Monday, the popular daily Bild called him the Sun King and used two full pages to tell his tale.
Cycling was one of few sports in which Germans, more passionate about four wheels with an engine than two without, have not fared too well up until now.
The last German to have worn the Tour leader's yellow jersey was Klaus Peter Thaler in 1978.
"Jan has written one of the most glorious pages in the history of German sports," said Dietrich Thurau, who rode with the coveted shirt on his back for 15 days in 1977.
Ullrich meanwhile said he needed time to realise what had happened to him. "It's all very sudden," he said.
The 23-year-old from the former East German city of Rostock qualifies as a true hero for the whole of Germany, an important point in the recently unified country.
Ullrich learned his trade in the sports schools of the former communist east and was regarded as a promising athlete before deciding to concentrate on cycling.
He was 14 when the Berlin Wall collapsed in 1989. Soon after unification in 1990, he moved to Hamburg and now lives in the quiet village of Merdingen, in the Black Forest.

Newspapers have been busy telling everything about him, from the size of his legs to the story of his trademark gold earring, which was given to him by Gaby, with whom he reportedly fell in love at first sight.
His mother Marianne was in tears after the Paris finish on Sunday, saying she was afraid her son might find it hard to maintain a semblance of a private life.
Certainly, Ullrich will have to get used to being a favourite with the local tabloids.
Telekom team manager Walter Godefroot reckons Ullrich could be king for some time to come. "He certainly has the talent to win a few more Tours," Godefroot said.
